name: One-Arm Pull-up / Chin-up
summary: Pulling pinnacle. Weighted → archer → assisted → negative → full OAC/OAP.

safety.notes: High elbow stress. Prefer chin-up (supinated) first for many athletes.

divergence_notes: CC demands very high two-arm volume first; FF uses +50% BW weighted pull as a key benchmark.

timeline.from_level: 12–15 strict pull-ups, a weighted pull-up at +25% bodyweight, 30s one-arm hang per side
timeline.human_label: 2–4+ years from 12–15 strict pull-ups, and a meaningful fraction of athletes never get there
timeline.notes: OG2 places the one-arm chin-up at the very top of the pulling chart. Bodyweight matters more here than on any other tree: the required weighted-pull-up standard scales directly with it, so heavier athletes face a compounding disadvantage. Elbow-tendon tolerance is the most common reason progress stops permanently rather than temporarily.

variance_drivers.note: Overrides the portfolio-wide bodyweight driver. A one-arm pull-up requires roughly a +80–100% bodyweight two-arm pull-up first; each extra kilogram raises that absolute target, so the same relative strength gain takes materially longer at higher bodyweights.

Rate of adaptation is logarithmic. An athlete with 3+ years of consistent resistance training moves through early steps in a fraction of the listed time but gains little advantage on the last two steps of any tree.
Connective tissue remodels more slowly with age. Athletes over ~40 should read the upper half of every band and extend tendon-conditioning steps rather than compressing them.
Longer arms and legs lengthen the lever at a fixed bodyweight. Taller athletes commonly need one extra intermediate shape (one-leg before straddle) that shorter athletes can skip.
Below roughly 2 quality sessions per week most athletes stall indefinitely on advanced steps. Gains from going beyond 4–5 sessions per week are small and injury risk rises (arampatzis-2024-loading).
Video review or a coach correcting shape is repeatedly reported to roughly halve time-to-skill on balance-dominant work versus unguided practice (kyleweiger-handstand).

prerequisite_standards.name: Strict pull-ups
prerequisite_standards.rationale: The conventional entry standard; below it the weighted work is not productive.

prerequisite_standards.name: Weighted pull-up
prerequisite_standards.rationale: The measurable bridge toward the roughly +80–100% bodyweight a one-arm pull-up demands.

prerequisite_standards.name: One-arm hang
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Grip and elbow-tendon tolerance for single-arm loading.

plateau_signatures.signal: Weighted pull-up stalls in the +40–50% bodyweight range for many months
typical_causes: This is the normal advanced plateau — ACSM puts advanced gains near 10% and elite near 2% over comparable periods
Volume too high to allow near-maximal quality
Bodyweight rising alongside strength, cancelling the relative gain
resolution: Switch to longer block progression rather than weekly increments
Cycle intensity rather than grinding maximal singles
Track relative strength (load plus bodyweight per kilogram) rather than absolute load

plateau_signatures.signal: Repeated cycles of progress followed by 4–8 weeks of elbow-driven backing off
typical_causes: Single-arm loading concentrates force on tendon structures that adapt on an 8–12 week clock while muscle adapts faster
resolution: Cap single-arm attempts per week regardless of how good they feel
Keep assisted and archer variants as the volume driver and reserve true one-arm work for low-rep quality

regression_triggers.trigger: Layoff or markedly reduced training for less than 4 weeks (illness, travel, work crunch)
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: No step lost. Hold times commonly return 10–25% short for the first two sessions; eccentric control and shape quality degrade before maximal strength does.
regression_triggers.action: Resume one step below your unlock for two sessions, then retest. Do not re-earn the whole step — strength-trained athletes show only limited decline at this timescale.

regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Force production falls roughly 7–12%, which usually costs one step on hold-based progressions and one to two steps on the hardest dynamic ones. Recently acquired gains are retained far better than the loss in maximal force suggests.
regression_triggers.action: Restart two steps below your previous unlock and rebuild with full volume but reduced intensity. Expect to regain the lost steps in a fraction of the time they originally took.

regression_triggers.trigger: Planned deload, or four consecutive weeks with no measurable progress
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: None. Hold times often improve in the week after the deload.
regression_triggers.action: Cut volume roughly in half and keep intensity, for one week. Overcoming Gravity's rule is that four weeks without progress means the cycle is finished, not that you need to try harder.

regression_triggers.trigger: Tendon pain forcing modified or stopped training
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Highly variable. Time lost is usually 6–12 weeks because the tissue must be reloaded from a low baseline, and the affected step is typically lost entirely.
regression_triggers.action: Drop to the last pain-free step, reintroduce isometric then slow eccentric loading, and rebuild across at least 8–12 weeks — the window in which tendon stiffness actually changes. Returning at the previous intensity is the most common cause of recurrence.

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Full bodyweight through one elbow, frequently at end-range extension at the start of the pull. The highest single-joint tendon load in the pulling trees.
prophylaxis: Keep a permanent base of high-rep two-arm and archer work
Never start a one-arm attempt from a cold dead hang
Respect at least 72h between true one-arm sessions
red_flags: Medial elbow pain at the start of the pull

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Asymmetric loading with a rotational component through a single shoulder
prophylaxis: Keep scapular control work in the programme permanently

productive.notes: Advanced trainees adapt on a monthly rather than weekly clock. Most of the weekly volume should come from assisted and archer variants; true one-arm work stays low-rep and high-quality.

too_much_signals: Any medial elbow discomfort between sessions
Grip failing before the lats on assisted work
Bodyweight climbing while relative strength stalls

deload.protocol: One week of two-arm work only at moderate load.
deload.trigger: Four weeks without progress, or any elbow symptom.
